steps.title: Give the GPU three corners
steps.goal: Draw a pink triangle on the white background.
steps.trace: Three shader positions → triangle coverage → fragment colour → canvas
steps.question: If you change the top vertex, which part of the picture changes, and which stays the same?
steps.answer: The triangle silhouette changes because its corner positions changed. The surrounding white stays the same: the render pass clears the background before drawing the triangle.

edits.why: Create GPU vertex and fragment functions; the vertex function chooses a corner and the fragment function returns pink.
Create and retain the triangle shader pipeline.
Bind the pipeline and draw its three vertices.
Pass the surface format to the renderer; a pipeline must agree with the texture it draws into.

steps.story:
Draw one pink triangle inside the white GPU frame. The shader supplies three corners; the renderer keeps one pipeline and records its draw.

The vertex shader places corners in clip space, where x and y near −1 and +1 reach the image edges. The fragment shader supplies colour. `0..3` draws three vertices; `0..1` draws one instance.

A pipeline is the reusable recipe connecting these shaders to the colour target. Keep it between frames. `include_str!` embeds the WGSL text at compile time. An empty vertex-buffer list means the shader still supplies its own positions; Rust will supply geometry in lesson 05. Use the same sRGB view format as browser presentation.

![Three corner positions form a triangle; a fragment shader colours its covered pixels.](../illustrations/journey-03.svg)
steps.result: A pink triangle appears on white. Change its top vertex in the shader, save, and check that only the triangle’s shape changes. Restore the vertex.
steps.experiment: Predict the result of changing the last corner from `(0.0, 0.6)` to `(0.4, 0.6)`. Run it: the top should move right while the base stays still. Then change only the fragment colour. Explain why that changes the inside colour but not the silhouette. Restore both edits.
steps.production: The production viewer also separates shader programs, pipeline setup and frame recording. Later mesh buffers replace the shader’s three hard-coded positions. We will make that replacement explicitly, after understanding what the positions do.

steps.title: Prepare the command fonts and painter
steps.goal: Create the font and GPU painter owner while keeping the triangle.
steps.trace: Embedded font bytes → shared font definitions → egui context → GPU painter
steps.question: Why can the font configuration keep the embedded byte slices?
steps.answer: include_bytes! supplies bytes with a static lifetime, so FontData can retain those slices. Arc lets egui share the same font data allocation; both families refer to its registered name.
steps.story:
Prepare one owner for the command drawing. It keeps an `egui::Context` and a GPU painter. The browser constructs this owner now; the triangle stays unchanged until we connect drawing.

`include_bytes!` embeds the three Noto font files in the program. Their static lifetime lets the font definitions retain them. `Arc` gives egui shared ownership of the font data; both families list the same font names. The `fonts` helper returns that configuration; `new` installs it, chooses the light theme and creates a painter using the existing device.

The painter records interface work on our GPU. It does not need a second canvas or HTML controls.

![The current command drawing step.](../illustrations/journey-03a-fonts.svg)
steps.result: The triangle stays visible in the full window. The font and painter owner is constructed, but no interface drawing is connected yet.
steps.experiment: Change visuals.window_fill and rebuild. Predict why the triangle stays unchanged before the painter is called, then restore the colour.
steps.production: This is the same Noto font setup and GPU painter used by the finished command dock.
steps.browser_caption: Chrome observes creation of the actual egui GPU shader and pipeline while the triangle stays unchanged. No interface is drawn yet.
steps.image_result: The native image checks the scene renderer; actual Chrome separately checks the interface drawing.

edits.why: Add egui and its GPU painter.
Keep the context and painter together.
Create the painter owner before presenting the scene.
Configure Noto fonts and the light theme.

steps.title: Paint command text over the scene
steps.goal: Draw a Command label over the triangle using the same GPU.
steps.trace: RawInput → egui shapes and font atlas → GPU upload → Load pass → present
steps.question: Why does the interface pass use Load?
steps.answer: The triangle is already in the target image. Load keeps those pixels while the interface draws over them; another Clear would erase the scene.
steps.story:
Draw the Command label after the triangle and before presenting the image. `RawInput` gives egui the available canvas size. `run_ui` calls our layout closure and returns shapes plus changed font-atlas pixels.

Upload those pixels, turn the shapes into triangle jobs and update their GPU buffers. The second render pass uses `Load`, so it keeps the scene pixels already drawn. The panel uses a white frame and the production margins.

`forget_lifetime` removes the pass’s compile-time link to the encoder. The pass still must end before we finish the encoder. Submit its buffers, then release textures egui no longer needs.

![The current command drawing step.](../illustrations/journey-03a-paint.svg)
steps.result: Command: appears at the bottom of the full-window canvas. The triangle remains unchanged above it. Keyboard input is not connected yet.
steps.experiment: Change only Load to a white Clear, rebuild and see which earlier drawing disappears. Restore Load.
steps.production: This introduces the interface upload and second GPU pass that the full command dock keeps.
steps.browser_status: Our command line is drawn. Input comes next.
steps.browser_caption: Chrome verifies visible Noto label ink, white panel pixels and exact preservation of the scene above the dock. Keyboard input is not connected.
steps.image_result: The native image checks the scene renderer; actual Chrome separately checks the interface drawing.

edits.why: Lay out the label, upload its font atlas and draw over the scene.
Create the panel and pass it into presentation.
Draw the panel over the scene before presenting.

[package]
name = "viewer_journey"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

[workspace]

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "=0.2.128"
web-sys = { version = "=0.3.105", features = ["Window", "Document", "Element", "HtmlCanvasElement", "EventTarget", "Event"] }

wasm-bindgen-futures = "=0.4.78"
wgpu = "=29.0.4"

egui = { version = "=0.34.3", default-features = false }
egui-wgpu = { version = "=0.34.3", default-features = false }

[dev-dependencies]
pollster = "=0.4.0"
log = "=0.4.34"
